title: The invoice that wasn't
summary: A fake overdue invoice reaches three people at Kestrel Logistics. One opens it. An hour later the HR and Finance folders are encrypted. Find patient zero, trace the attack, contain it and choose a backup to restore.
ctf: The loader's campaign value hides a flag (step 7). Submit it on the CTF board as "The invoice that wasn't".

template.s:
# Incident runbook: ransomware at Kestrel Logistics

09:55, Monday 2 Nov. The helpdesk pulled the network cable on **hr-pc07** after files on the shared drive started ending in `.kestrel-locked`. You lead the response.

The evidence is in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python). the network tools (`nmap`, `curl`, `wget`, `tshark`, `dig`, `nslookup`, `host`, `whois`, `ping`, `traceroute`, `nc`, `ssh`, `openssl`, `nikto`, `gobuster`) work on a recorded copy of the case network; nothing leaves your browser.

The steps follow the incident response lifecycle: **verify, scope, find the way in, preserve evidence, contain, eradicate, recover, learn**. The order is based on the open LetsDefend incident response playbooks (MIT licence).

### What you'll learn

- Read email headers to find the real sender, and spot a look-alike domain
- Match a proxy log and a process tree to find patient zero
- Decode a base64 loader setting and check files against threat intel
- Measure how far ransomware spread and choose a clean backup

### How to use this runbook

- Run a cell with **Shift+Enter** (or its Run button). Run the cells in order: the first Linux cell copies the evidence into `~/case`.
- Tick each `- [ ]` box when you have done it.
- Stuck? Open a **Hint** under the step.
- Type your answer into each **check** box and it tells you if you are right. Answers are short: an address, a name, a number or a time such as 09:05.
- Write your notes under each step. Download .ipynb keeps your notes and every output.

## 1. Triage

- [ ] Write your name and the time you started here:
- [ ] Hash the evidence before you touch it
- [ ] Read the ransom note: what do the attackers want?
- [ ] Map the network

> Hint: `ls -l` lists the files, `sha256sum` prints a fingerprint for each one. Save those hashes before you open anything.
> Hint: The ransom note and the share listing both name the extension the ransomware adds to every file.
?> Which file extension does the ransomware add? (include the dot) :: sha256:7267b77d0ef78e40d9e82eb6495f6658e7ddda42fd7ba893109e37961d6af7a5
?> How many hosts does `nmap -sn 10.20.0.0/24` find up? :: sha256:7902699be42c8a8e46fbbb4501726517e86b22c56a189f7625a6da49081b2451

cd ~/case
ls -l . suspect
sha256sum *.* suspect/*
echo ---
cat README_RESTORE.txt

## 2. Verify: is this real?

Alerts are often wrong. Before you wake anyone up, decide whether this is a **true positive**.

- [ ] What exactly raised the alarm, and when?
- [ ] Name two pieces of evidence that prove something bad really happened
- [ ] What harmless explanation would make this a false positive? Can you rule it out?
- [ ] Decision: true positive / false positive (write it here)

> Hint: A true positive needs evidence, not a feeling. Look for something only an attacker would do, such as a file that should not exist or a connection to an address nobody uses.
?> How many files in `share_listing.txt` end in .kestrel-locked? :: sha256:4a44dc15364204a80fe80e9039455cc1608281820fe2b24f1e5233ade6af1dd5

## 3. The email

- [ ] Who really sent it? Compare `From`, `Reply-To`, `Return-Path` and the `Received` line
- [ ] What did SPF, DKIM and DMARC say?
- [ ] Spot the look-alike domain: which letter is wrong?
- [ ] What does the real domain publish in DNS?
- [ ] List the pressure tactics in the message (Unit 1.1)

> Hint: The `Received` line is added by your own mail server, so the attacker can't fake it. The address in square brackets is the real sender.
> Hint: Read the two domains letter by letter: kestrel-logist**i**cs and kestrel-logist**l**cs.
?> Which IP address really sent the email? :: sha256:eb4b2dd34d5ba9aff5f39480c21f10aff75f58d1bfe56c0d153cb60b63533992
?> Which letter replaced the i in the look-alike domain? :: sha256:acac86c0e609ca906f632b0e2dacccb2b77d22b0621f20ebece1a4835b93f6f0
?> What DMARC policy does the real domain publish? (the word after p=) :: sha256:084e990a49ba65e622926853785e0ed05c63fc7fbf798a26e8242b5ee3d7ce9f

grep -E '^(From|Reply-To|Return-Path|Received|Subject|Authentication-Results)' -A1 invoice.eml
echo ---
dig +short kestrel-logistics.com
dig TXT kestrel-logistics.com +short
dig TXT _dmarc.kestrel-logistics.com +short
echo ---
dig +short kestrel-logistlcs.com
dig TXT kestrel-logistlcs.com +short
dig -x 203.0.113.45 +short
echo ---
whois kestrel-logistlcs.com
whois kestrel-logistics.com | head -3

## 4. Who got it, and who clicked?

- [ ] How many people received the email?
- [ ] Who reported it, and when?
- [ ] Which computers downloaded the invoice? Did the block stop anyone?

The proxy log times are Unix epoch seconds. The Python cell turns them into clock times.

> Hint: `nrcpt=` in mail.log is the number of recipients. In proxy.log, TCP_MISS/200 means the download worked and TCP_DENIED/403 means the proxy blocked it.
?> How many people received the email? :: sha256:4e07408562bedb8b60ce05c1decfe3ad16b72230967de01f640b7e4729b49fce
?> Which internal IP address downloaded the invoice successfully? :: sha256:ecda40e9a719dbe5a19ca890028508dc0dffab4ef41d0accd82d2c3a46a8405d
?> At what time (HH:MM, UTC) did that download happen? :: sha256:b14795fe960de9648774c15eac13483db8adce7aefa63462eb0cea308987d95e

grep 4A1F21C02 mail.log
grep -E 'report|blocklist' mail.log
echo ---
grep -E 'docm|s2.bin' proxy.log

from datetime import datetime, timezone

for line in open("case/proxy.log"):
    f = line.split()
    when = datetime.fromtimestamp(float(f[0]), timezone.utc).strftime("%H:%M:%S")
    print(when, f[2], f[3], f[5], f[6])

## 5. What ran on hr-pc07?

- [ ] Rebuild the process tree from `process.csv`
- [ ] Which program started PowerShell? Why is that suspicious?
- [ ] Where does the real `svchost.exe` live, and who starts it? Where does this one live?

> Hint: Follow the ppid column: each process names its parent. Word should never start cmd.exe; a macro did that.
> Hint: The real svchost.exe lives in C:\Windows\System32 and runs as SYSTEM. Look for one with a slightly different name in a public folder.
?> Which program started cmd.exe? (file name) :: sha256:f8878dc09ca0bd8005c9009ae3a4aee3085d3081b5c95e2232c9d8e561ce9166
?> What is the PID of the svchost-upd.exe that PowerShell started? :: sha256:cfe35c9e498096d4463cfade00cdef305d2311d90db9949bf321f87447fc2f1a

import csv
from collections import defaultdict

rows = [r for r in csv.DictReader(open("case/process.csv")) if r["host"] == "hr-pc07"]
kids = defaultdict(list)
for r in rows:
    kids[r["ppid"]].append(r)

def show(pid, depth):
    for r in kids.get(pid, []):
        print("    " * depth + r["time"][11:] + "  " + r["image"].split("\\")[-1] + "  " + r["command_line"][:70])
        show(r["pid"], depth + 1)

show("704", 0)
show("640", 0)

## 6. The network

- [ ] Which names did hr-pc07 look up, and when?
- [ ] What did it download, and with what user agent?
- [ ] How often does it call home on port 443?
- [ ] When did the encryption over SMB start and stop?

> Hint: Subtract the times of the TLS Client Hello packets to the command server. A steady gap is a beacon.
?> How many seconds pass between the beacons on port 443? :: sha256:983bd614bb5afece5ab3b6023f71147cd7b6bc2314f9d27af7422541c6558389
?> Which domain did hr-pc07 look up right after the invoice download? :: sha256:c34fa70e89a7709bcc132bd0e2520092c83206a1e769718af097fa5e2d62f2ec

tshark -r capture.pcap -Y dns -T fields -e frame.time_relative -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name
echo ---
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.user_agent
echo ---
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'tls and ip.src==10.20.0.14' -T fields -e frame.time_relative
echo ---
tshark -r capture.pcap -Y smb2 | head -12
tshark -r capture.pcap -q -z conv,ip

## 7. Take the loader apart

The macro wrote a settings file before it fetched the ransomware. Its `campaign=` value is base64.

- [ ] Decode the campaign value. What is in it? (There is a CTF flag in there.)
- [ ] Match the files against the threat intel feed
- [ ] Read the strings pulled from the ransomware: which folder does it target?
- [ ] Are the attacker's servers still up?

> Hint: `cut -d= -f2-` keeps everything after the first `=`, and `base64 -d` decodes it. The fields are separated by `|`.
> Hint: The flag is the last field of the decoded value. Submit it on the CTF board, not here.
?> Which port is the second field of the decoded campaign value? :: sha256:6d05621ab7cb7b4fb796ca2ffbe1a141e0d4319d3deb6a05322b9de85d69b923
?> Which file in `suspect/` is on the threat intel feed? (file name only) :: sha256:b266aef728bf88ac568e36113bb53d570b3461c5e215418a809ebcbaf0b4ec00

cat suspect/upd.cfg
echo ---
grep '^campaign=' suspect/upd.cfg | cut -d= -f2- | base64 -d; echo
echo ---
sha256sum suspect/* | while read h f; do
    grep -q "$h" known_bad.txt && echo "KNOWN BAD: $f" || echo "not listed: $f"
done
grep -E 'fs01|kestrel-locked|cdn' suspect/svchost-upd.strings.txt

curl -I http://kestrel-logistlcs.com/invoices/INV-30412.docm
curl -s http://cdn-update-check.net/api/v1/hello
nmap -sV 198.51.100.140
openssl s_client -connect cdn-update-check.net:443 | grep -E 'subject=|issuer=|NotBefore|Verify'
nc -zv 198.51.100.140 440-445

## 8. How far did it get?

- [ ] Which folders were encrypted, and in what time window?
- [ ] Which folder was saved by pulling the cable?
- [ ] Why could one HR laptop encrypt Finance's files? Scan the file server.

> Hint: The awk line counts locked files per folder. A folder with no locked files was saved.
?> Which folder on the share was not encrypted? :: sha256:a92c36e66a25ee99ff862faa8e87987be6c7cd13c3ee661c400a45b0f1e3b132
?> At what time (HH:MM) was the last file encrypted? :: sha256:a0b059528bee3eb374974bcf3cb583eb5ba29b7607b3346136fbff698bfe7a33

awk '/Directory of/ {d = $3} /kestrel-locked/ {n[d]++} END {for (k in n) print n[k], "locked in", k}' share_listing.txt
grep kestrel-locked share_listing.txt | awk '{print $2}' | sort | sed -n '1p;$p'
echo ---
nmap -sV fs01.kestrel.lan

## 9. Initial access: how did they get in?

The way in is the door you must close, or it happens again. Tick the one the evidence supports, and write the evidence next to it.

- [ ] Phishing (a message that tricked someone)
- [ ] Exploit of a public-facing application (a website or service bug)
- [ ] Valid accounts (a real username and password or key, stolen or misused)
- [ ] External remote services (VPN, remote desktop, SSH)
- [ ] Drive-by compromise (a booby-trapped website)
- [ ] Supply chain or trusted partner
- [ ] Hardware added (a USB device or rogue machine)
- [ ] Insider using access they were given
- [ ] No intrusion (for example, traffic from outside that never got in)

## 10. Preserve the evidence

Cleaning up destroys evidence. Copy everything to a safe place, record the hashes and pack it before you change anything.

- [ ] Copy the evidence and write SHA256SUMS
- [ ] Note who collected it, when, and where it is stored (chain of custody)

mkdir -p ~/evidence && cp -r ~/case/* ~/evidence/
cd ~/evidence && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS -exec sha256sum {} + > SHA256SUMS
pack=~/evidence-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M).tar
tar cf "$pack" -C ~/evidence .
(gzip -f "$pack" 2>/dev/null && echo "packed $pack.gz") || echo "packed $pack"
ls -l ~/evidence-*
wc -l SHA256SUMS
cd ~/case

## 11. Contain

- [ ] Keep hr-pc07 off the network, but don't switch it off yet (memory evidence)
- [ ] Block the look-alike domain and the command server everywhere
- [ ] Reset priya.nair's password and sign her out everywhere
- [ ] Search every mailbox for the same message and delete it

The cell prints the commands. Nothing here touches a real firewall.

for d in kestrel-logistlcs.com cdn-update-check.net; do echo "dns-block add $d"; done
echo "iptables -A OUTPUT -d 198.51.100.140 -j DROP"
echo "iptables -A FORWARD -s 10.20.0.14 -j DROP"
echo "mail-purge --message-id '20261102085103.7781@kestrel-logistlcs.com' --all-mailboxes"

## 12. Recover

- [ ] Which snapshot is the last clean one? Why not the newest?
- [ ] How much work is lost (the RPO)?
- [ ] What is wrong with how the backups are stored? How would you fix it?
- [ ] Two lasting fixes: block macros in files from the internet, and limit which folders each team can write to

> Hint: s-1102 was taken at 23:00 on 2 Nov, after the attack at 09:41. Its files are already locked.
?> Which snapshot is the last clean one? (its ID) :: sha256:54d426929fbfcfb9e645760fd9320fdf02b87605cc31b7922cee292085439f0b
cat backups.txt

- [ ] What went well (a user reported it) and what to fix

Write the report here. Download .ipynb keeps every output above.
